title: CVE-2026-21589: Critical Pre-Authentication File Read Affects Atlassian Data Center Products
content:
Atlassian has released an out-of-band security advisory for CVE-2026-21589, a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability affecting a broad range of its Data Center products. The flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and can be exploited remotely without authentication or user interaction. Because vulnerable functionality is shared across the Atlassian product ecosystem, every previous version of the affected products is impacted.

An attacker who knows the exact name and path of a file can use the vulnerability to read it from within the affected application’s web root. The issue does not provide directory-listing or file-enumeration capabilities, but many Atlassian deployments follow predictable directory structures. This can make sensitive configuration files practical targets even without prior access to the system.

Atlassian released fixed versions on October 5, 2026, and urged Data Center customers to patch immediately. Atlassian Cloud environments have already been patched, and Atlassian said its investigation had not identified evidence of exploitation affecting Cloud customers at the time of disclosure.

What Is CVE-2026-21589?

CVE-2026-21589 is an unauthenticated path traversal vulnerability in Atlassian’s web-resource handling. Research traced the flaw to the shared atlassian-plugins-webresource component. Vulnerable code converts double-colon sequences (::) into forward slashes when resolving requested resources. In affected routes, crafted traversal sequences can pass through path-processing logic and reach files within the application server’s web root.

The attack does not require a valid Atlassian account. A remote attacker can submit a specially crafted HTTP request to a vulnerable instance and retrieve a file if its location is known. The technique has been demonstrated against Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket, with product-specific request paths leading to protected files under the applications’ WEB-INF directories.

The direct result is unauthorized file disclosure rather than remote code execution. However, the practical impact depends heavily on the files stored in the web root and the way Atlassian products are integrated. Configuration files may contain credentials, internal service locations, or other information that enables further compromise.

From File Read to Administrative Access

Atlassian’s documented Jira–Crowd configuration stores the Crowd application name, application password, and server URL in WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties. In a vulnerable and permissively configured deployment, an attacker could use CVE-2026-21589 to retrieve this file and obtain the credentials used by Jira to communicate with Crowd. The researchers showed that those credentials could then be used to interact with Crowd’s user-management API, create a user, and add that account to the jira-administrators group.

This escalation path is configuration-dependent. Crowd can restrict access by source IP, which may make direct use of leaked credentials more difficult. Even so, the demonstrated chain shows why a file-read vulnerability can have consequences well beyond the disclosure of application files: secrets exposed from one Atlassian product may provide a path into the identity layer shared by the wider environment.

Affected Atlassian Products and Fixed Versions

All versions released before the following fixed versions are affected:

Product Fixed versions
Bitbucket Data Center 9.4.26, 10.2.8, 10.5.1
Confluence Data Center 9.2.26, 10.2.19
Jira Service Management Data Center 5.12.40, 10.3.26, 11.3.12
Jira Software Data Center 9.12.40, 10.3.26, 11.3.12
Bamboo Data Center 10.2.24, 12.1.12
Crowd Data Center 6.3.7, 7.0.3, 7.1.7, 7.2.4
Crucible 4.9.15
Fisheye 4.9.15

Atlassian recommends upgrading to one of the listed fixed releases or a later version. Organizations should verify every node in a clustered deployment, as well as Bitbucket mirrors and mirror-farm nodes where applicable.

What Imperva Is Seeing

Imperva telemetry shows that detection activity associated with CVE-2026-21589 has been heavily concentrated among targets in Singapore, which accounted for 86.8% of observed activity.

The telecommunications and internet service provider sector was the primary target, accounting for 68% of observed activity. The concentration in telecommunications and ISP environments is notable because Atlassian products frequently support internal development, operations, and service-management workflows in large, interconnected organizations.

Mitigation and Detection

Patching is the primary remediation. Atlassian advises customers to upgrade each affected installation to a fixed version or the latest available release. If patching cannot be completed immediately, Atlassian recommends removing affected instances from public internet access until a patch or temporary mitigation is in place.

For threat hunting, Atlassian recommends reviewing access logs for traversal sequences. Request lines should be URL-decoded up to two times before searching for .. adjacent to /, \, or ::. Security teams can also search decoded logs using the regular expression published in Atlassian’s advisory. Because exploitation requires a known path, requests referencing WEB-INF, web.xml, urlrewrite.xml, crowd.properties, or other sensitive application files warrant particular scrutiny.

Organizations using Crowd integrations should also consider the potential exposure of application credentials. If logs or other evidence indicate that a sensitive configuration file may have been retrieved, incident response should extend beyond patching the vulnerable Atlassian instance to include credential rotation, review of Crowd users and group memberships, and investigation of activity across connected products.

How Imperva Helps

Imperva Web Application Firewall helps identify and block malicious path-traversal requests before they reach vulnerable Atlassian applications. Its inspection of decoded and obfuscated request paths is relevant to CVE-2026-21589 because exploitation can use nonstandard separators and encoded traversal patterns to reach protected files.

Customers should still install Atlassian’s fixed releases as soon as possible. A WAF provides an important compensating control while upgrades are tested and deployed, but it does not replace remediation of the vulnerable software or investigation of possible earlier access.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-21589 combines a low-complexity, unauthenticated attack path with an unusually broad affected-product footprint. Although the immediate capability is limited to reading known files within the application web root, predictable file locations and shared credentials can turn that access into a much larger identity and administrative compromise.

While Imperva customers are protected out-of-the-box, all organizations running Atlassian Data Center products should treat the issue as an emergency: inventory affected installations, patch every node to a fixed release, apply Atlassian’s temporary mitigations where patching is delayed, and review historical access logs for traversal patterns and requests targeting sensitive configuration files.
